title: Yield & atom economy
examples: How do I calculate the percent yield if I only have the actual mass?
What is the difference between percent yield and atom economy?
Can you show me an example where the atom economy is zero?

explain.say: Today we learn about percent yield in chemical reactions. This tells us how much product we actually get.
The theoretical yield is the maximum amount we expect to make. We calculate this using balanced equations.
Atom economy measures how many atoms from the reactants end up in the desired product. It is a measure of efficiency.

draw.text: Atom Economy = (Mass of Desired Product / Total Reactants) x 100

explain.say: If a reaction produces waste, the atom economy will be less than one hundred percent. This means some atoms are wasted.
A low percent yield suggests something went wrong in the lab. Maybe the product was lost or the reaction didn't complete.

draw.text: Low Yield: Loss or Incomplete Reaction

explain.say: In everyday life, baking a cake shows this idea well. The recipe gives the theoretical amount, but you might get less.

faq.q: What is the difference between percent yield and atom economy?
faq.a: Percent yield compares what you actually get to what you should get. Atom economy compares the mass of the product to the total mass of all starting materials.
asks: Are they both measures of efficiency?
Do I use moles or grams for each calculation?

faq.q: If the atom economy is one hundred percent, what does that mean?
faq.a: It means every single atom from the starting materials ends up in the final desired product. There is no waste product formed.
asks: Is a 100 percent atom economy perfect?
Does this mean the reaction is easy to perform?

faq.q: Can a reaction have a percent yield of zero?
faq.a: Yes, if no product is formed at all, the actual yield would be zero. This means the reaction failed completely.
asks: What causes a zero percent yield?
Is zero yield the same as no reaction?

faq.q: Do I need to balance the equation before calculating atom economy?
faq.a: Yes, you must always balance the chemical equation first. Stoichiometry relies on the correct mole ratios from the balanced equation.
asks: Is balancing the equation important for yield?
Should I use the coefficients in the calculation?

faq.q: If my actual yield is less than the theoretical yield, what should I check?
faq.a: You should check for potential sources of product loss. This could be spillage, incomplete drying, or side reactions occurring.
asks: Why is my actual yield lower than expected?
What causes the difference between the two yields?

facts: Percent yield is calculated by dividing the actual mass by the theoretical mass.
Atom economy considers the mass of all atoms in the desired product versus all reactants.
A reaction with 100 percent atom economy is considered ideal in theory.
Low percent yield often points to experimental error or side reactions.

quiz.say: For the reaction A + B → C + D, if the total mass of A and B is 100 grams and the desired product C has a total mass of 60 grams, what is the atom economy?
quiz.why: Atom economy compares the mass of the desired product (60 grams) to the total mass of all starting materials (100 grams).

wrong.0: Calculating the mass of the waste product (D) and using that number.
wrong.1: Adding the mass of the desired product to the waste product.
wrong.2: Assuming all atoms must end up in the desired product.

quiz.say: Which scenario suggests the lowest atom economy?

options.show: The reaction produces a large amount of waste.
options.say: The reaction produces a large amount of waste.

options.show: The reaction has a low percent yield.
options.say: The reaction has a low percent yield.

quiz.why: Atom economy is low when a large proportion of the starting material ends up as waste rather than the desired product.

wrong.1: Low percent yield relates to physical loss, not necessarily chemical waste atoms.
wrong.2: The total mass of reactants does not determine the atom economy value.
wrong.3: The mass of the product alone is not enough information; the waste mass must also be considered.
